body.text: Attribution: Manini, “The Impact of CBAM’s Extension to Downstream Products on MSMEs,” ORF Issue Brief No. 902, Observer Research Foundation, October 2026.

Modern manufacturing increasingly relies on complex raw materials and global supply chains, making production both transnational and energy intensive. Much of this energy use is accompanied by carbon emissions. For instance, the steel industry alone is responsible for 2.8 gigatonnes, or 8 percent, of energy-related CO₂ emissions annually.[1] These emissions occur far from where final products and services are consumed. This is particularly evident in steel value chains, where value is realised in downstream products such as machinery or construction materials, while much of the energy use and carbon emissions occur upstream during iron ore reduction, blast furnace operations, and steel processing. These processes rely heavily on coal and electricity: around 90 percent of iron production today uses coal-fired blast furnaces, while alternatives such as natural gas, hydrogen, biochar, and direct electrification account for around 10 percent of iron production.[2],[3] As a result, the environmental cost of production is often far removed from the point of consumption, both geographically and economically.

In sectors such as steel and aluminium, much of the pollution is generated in upstream applications, while the value of goods and services is realised later in downstream manufactured products. The gap creates risks of unfair competition and carbon leakage. Producers in countries with little to no carbon pricing can then export goods to countries with stringent carbon pricing and rules, without paying the comparable environmental cost. To address this imbalance, the European Union (EU) designed the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM),[4] which assigns a carbon price on emissions embedded in goods imported into the EU.

CBAM was originally conceived to prevent carbon leakage by ensuring that foreign producers of carbon-intensive goods face carbon costs similar to those borne by EU firms under the Emissions Trading System (ETS). Even at this stage, the mechanism placed a disproportionate burden on micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) exporting to the EU. While a 150-euro shipment threshold and a 50-tonne annual de-minimis clause limit were originally added to shield small EU importers from administrative burdens, MSME exporters continued to bear hidden compliance costs and trade disruptions.[5] Take the engineering goods sector, for instance. In 2022–23, MSMEs comprised nearly 20 percent of India’s exports in this segment, valued at over US$24 billion.[6]

Many of the Indian MSME firms operate in industrial clusters such as Rajkot, Coimbatore, and Mandi Gobindgarh. These clusters are home to small foundries and rolling mills, many of which still rely on coal-based production.[7] On paper, some of these firms fall below the EU’s 50-tonne CBAM reporting threshold. In practice, however, the exemption offers limited protection. Export shipments are often consolidated by merchant exporters or intermediaries, and this can push consignments above the threshold. At the same time, large buyers and Tier-1 suppliers are increasingly asking for emissions data from their suppliers. This pressure moves down the supply chain. As a result, many Tier-2 and Tier-3 MSMEs must begin reporting emissions even when they are not directly covered by CBAM rules. [8],[9]

Proposals to extend CBAM coverage to downstream steel and aluminium products, and discussions to recycle CBAM revenues to support EU industries during the transition so they can compete with outside producers, signal a possible shift in the mechanism’s industrial objectives.[10],[11] This is particularly concerning because the shift comes at a critical time: the CBAM’s transition phase ended in 2025, after which importers became subject to full financial liabilities, coinciding with the gradual phase-out of free ETS allowances for EU producers.[12]

To say the least, CBAM is increasingly embedded within the EU’s broader industrial competitiveness and trade defence strategy, rather than functioning solely as a climate tool. However, in the longer term, there are risks of mismatching the site of emissions and who bears the cost. This fundamentally alters incentives not just for raw material producers, but also for value chains. Instead of targeting a limited number of upstream producers, the extension pushes carbon pricing deeper into manufacturing value chains. This will directly affect MSMEs. Many of them operate in later stages of metal processing, fabrication, re-rolling, and component manufacturing.[13],[14] These firms are often linked to export supply chains, which makes them more exposed to CBAM.

This brief examines the implications of extending CBAM downstream and how this may reshape incentives across manufacturing value chains. It outlines which actors are likely to gain or lose, and whether the current design risks the de-facto exclusion of MSMEs from EU-linked markets.

CBAM currently applies to basic material goods like iron and steel, aluminium, cement, electricity, fertilisers, and hydrogen.[15] Producers that use these materials as input to manufacture goods further down the value chain (downstream goods) can face increased costs. This comes from the gradual phase-in of CBAM and the phasing out of ETS free allowances. This means that firms could partially circumvent carbon costs by shifting emissions-intensive processing stages. This includes the shifting of stages such as rolling or forming outside of the EU, while continuing to access the EU market through downstream goods. This could lead to “value chain leakage” and “resource shuffling”. Acknowledging this risk, the European Commission proposed a revised CBAM framework incorporating explicit anti-circumvention provisions and an extension of the scope to selected downstream products.[16] This ensures that imported products pay a similar price to goods produced within the EU.

In the proposal, a total of 180 downstream steel and aluminium products have been added to the scope of CBAM.[17] This includes semi-finished and finished goods, of which 94 percent are industrial supply chain products and the rest are household goods, such as washing machines.[18] For example, fabricated metals (nails, furniture fittings), machinery (pumps, engines, robots, household appliances like fridges), vehicles (chassis, parts), medical instruments, and metal furniture, in which steel or aluminium inputs constitute a large share (79 percent on average) of embedded emissions.[19]

When CBAM applies only to primary materials such as steel or aluminium, compliance is largely concentrated among a limited number of upstream producers. Extending CBAM coverage downstream introduces manifold measurement and governance challenges that do not arise at the upstream level. Eventually, as the scope expands across the value chain and affects multiple stages of the manufacturing value chain, a much larger set of actors becomes involved. Importers of machinery, vehicle equipment, and metal components will all become CBAM operators on paper.[20] However, in practice, downstream extension shifts compliance burdens onto firms that neither control upstream energy choices nor have the capacity to decarbonise them, particularly MSMEs.

Competitiveness in these sectors will be shaped less by emissions intensity alone and more by firms’ capacity to measure, report, and verify embedded emissions across suppliers. This may reduce risks of ‘value chain leakage’; however, it also raises new distributional concerns. Given that CBAM information must be submitted separately for each product and for every production facility, emissions accounting becomes more complex when CBAM moves downstream.[21] Therefore, measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) requirements expand across supply chains rather than increasing gradually. Small suppliers often lack the technical capacity to measure process-level emissions. Many also struggle to access standardised data formats compatible with EU reporting systems as well as dedicated legal or compliance teams to manage CBAM documentation.[22] Compliance costs and administrative burdens are unlikely to be evenly distributed, which creates structural advantages for large firms.

Alongside the downstream extension, the European Commission has also proposed using CBAM revenues to support EU producers facing higher costs from carbon pricing. The proposed Temporary Decarbonisation Fund (TCF) reflects pressure from the domestic industry. Firms are concerned about losing competitiveness in third markets as ETS-free allowances start phasing out.[23]

TCF will now account for only 25 percent of CBAM certificate sales revenues in 2026 and 2027. The remaining 75 percent will remain within the EU budget.[24] This form of revenue recycling will create a real policy tension: revenues collected at the border would be channelled back into the domestic economy to cushion EU firms. While CBAM is meant to put a price on carbon and encourage cleaner production, directing financial support to the same firms only questions the ambitions. Supporting carbon-intensive firms, even temporarily, may shift emissions abroad instead of reducing them. It can unfairly disadvantage firms that do not rely on such compensation.

While CBAM is designed and justified as a climate tool, its implementation as a trade measure at the border presents a contradiction. CBAM, as a climate tool, fails to abide by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR). This provision recognises that developed and developing countries have different historical responsibilities for emissions and different capacities to respond.[25] Meanwhile, as a trade measure, it struggles to comply with the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) non-discrimination rules. CBAM has been raising WTO concerns for being a competitive industrial tool flagged as green. However, revenue recycling through TCF further sharpens this contradiction.

India formally voiced objections against CBAM 29 times at the WTO between 2020 and 2024.[26] In May 2025, Russia initiated a formal WTO dispute against CBAM, citing violations of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) 1994 and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (SCM).[27] The Kazan Declaration, signed by BRICS countries, outrightly rejected CBAM for being a protectionist, unilateral trade barrier that undermines global climate and trade standards.[28] A country already paying for CBAM compliance should not compete in the same market as an EU industry that receives subsidies.

While EU producers get a temporary export support mechanism to adjust, many MSMEs in exporting countries—which are now pulled into CBAM’s net through the downstream extension—do not get an equivalent cushion under CBAM.[29],[30] They bear the compliance burden with no equivalent safety net. When environmental and legal costs are not evenly distributed, it creates an asymmetry. Thus, revenue recycling not only questions climate credibility but also deepens the distributional problem that downstream CBAM already creates for smaller firms.

The downstream extension of CBAM will not affect all firms in the same way: it is likely to benefit large and capital-intensive firms, while placing disproportionate burdens on MSMEs. This gap is not driven by differences in emissions performance alone; instead, it reflects differences in administrative capacity and financial ability, as well as market control. Large firms may be more exposed to international competition; however, they are also far better equipped to comply with CBAM requirements. They usually have dedicated compliance teams and access to consultants. They also tend to have clearer investment plans and stronger links with policymakers. Otherwise, they are still more able to absorb short-term compliance costs, such as by investing in data systems or managing temporary increases in input prices. Their scale allows them to spread these costs across production and pass some of them on to consumers.

MSMEs, on the other hand, face a very different situation. Under downstream CBAM, compliance costs can be high on a per-unit basis, particularly due to the administrative and technical burdens. For firms with limited cash flow, these costs are difficult to absorb. Many MSMEs depend on upstream suppliers for emissions data and reporting tools. However, they have little bargaining power to demand standardised information. They also have limited flexibility to rapidly change production processes.[31] As a result, accurate reporting becomes difficult, and many firms fall back on default values, which typically assume higher emissions and push up their CBAM costs further. Take India, for example, where MSMEs account for nearly 46 percent of the country’s exports. Many are deeply rooted in EU-linked supply chains, often as Tier-2 and Tier-3 suppliers.[32] The 150-euro shipment threshold and a 50-tonne annual de-minimis limit exist on paper. In practice, these thresholds are too low to cover most commercial consignments.[33],[34]

Since mandatory CBAM emissions reporting began in October 2023, importers have had to submit quarterly reports on embedded emissions. For many Indian exporters, especially MSMEs, this has proven too complex. Some small and mid-sized firms have already suspended shipments to the EU due to compliance difficulties.[35] Between FY2024 and FY2025, India’s steel and aluminium exports to the EU fell by 24.4 percent, dropping from US$7.71 billion to US$5.82 billion.[36] Steel was hit the most, with iron and steel exports plummeting by 35.1 percent to US$3.05 billion. Aluminium exports dropped by 9.8 percent.[37] The decline materialised even before CBAM tax collection began in 2026.

Part of the explanation lies in how India’s steel sector is structured. Primary steel production through the blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace route is highly carbon-intensive and controlled by a few large firms.[38] Most MSMEs operate in the secondary steel sector, including induction furnace and electric arc furnace routes. Together, they comprise about 55 percent of output and rely heavily on coal-based direct reduced iron (DRI).[39] Over 1,200 small and medium steel re-rolling mills produce around 33 million tonnes each year and support about 400,000 jobs.[40] Coal-based DRI already accounts for 37 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of output.[41] Under the National Steel Policy 2017, this could expand to 80 MTPA by 2030, with 70 percent of this expansion still expected to remain coal-based.[42] This puts nearly 80 percent of bar exports at risk under EU carbon rules.[43]

In practice, the EU has gone a step further by placing pre-consumer metal scrap under the CBAM framework.[45] At the same time, the EU may tighten scrap metal exports to support its domestic circular economy, such that scrap does not leave the country.[46] Taken together, these measures risk creating a de-facto exclusion of MSMEs from EU-linked value chains. This is not because they resist decarbonisation; many simply lack the resources to shift quickly to low- or zero-carbon production.[47]

The downstream extension of CBAM adds new challenges for MSMEs. However, it may also open up limited opportunities for firms that adapt early. There is opportunity in the early adoption of carbon-transparent production practices.[48] As CBAM requirements spread across value chains, large EU buyers and leading firms will increasingly seek suppliers who can provide basic emissions data. MSMEs that invest early in simple emissions tracking or cleaner inputs may gain preferred supplier status. This implies that they may spend less on purchasing carbon credits and may gain an edge over higher-emitting rivals. They may also find it easier to access EU green public procurement markets,[49] where carbon reporting is becoming a standard requirement.

Second, as CBAM requirements expand, firms will need support with emissions measurement, data management, verification, reporting, and certification. This has led to the growth of private consulting and reporting services that help firms meet CBAM’s MRV requirements. Consulting firms such as KPMG and EY, along with CBAM reporting software like Maverick, Sinai, and Sphera, now offer services to calculate emissions and manage CBAM reporting.[50],[51],[52],[53] Large firms can use these tools and services to lower compliance burdens by outsourcing complex reporting. For MSMEs, however, this new layer often acts as an expensive middleman. Many small manufacturers lack the knowledge or resources to judge which tools or platforms are reliable.

There is currently no EU-wide system to certify CBAM service providers, and this raises concerns around cost and uneven access. At the same time, it may create demand for new services linked to emissions transparency. In India, CleanCarbon is one such platform that has gained traction. The government-backed ‘Carbon Cell’ initiative, launched by the Services Export Promotion Council (SEPC) in partnership with CleanCarbon.ai, aims to support Indian MSMEs with CBAM reporting. [54] While helpful, such platforms also highlight how compliance risks are increasingly shifting from public regulators to private actors, thereby opening space for smaller firms to participate as manufacturers and service providers for MSMEs. These markets remain underdeveloped, but they could grow quickly if CBAM requirements become more stable and predictable.
However, these opportunities will only materialise if firms have access to training and affordable verification. Without this support, the benefits are more likely to go to larger firms.

Measuring and reporting emissions should be made simpler and affordable for small firms. While large companies may be able to track emissions at the factory level, this is often unrealistic for small manufacturers. Reporting standards should therefore be adjusted based on company size or export volumes to ease the disclosure burden. MSMEs should be allowed to use default emissions values, with the option to move to verified actual values as their capacity improves. At the same time, governments should also subsidise the cost of emissions reporting for MSMEs, provide easy-to-use accounting tools, and set up a one-stop digital CBAM platform for data compliance to support exporters with CBAM reporting.

India, with other countries, could petition that instead of mainly compensating large EU exporters, a share of CBAM revenues could be redirected to support MSMEs. This could fund basic emissions measurement tools, shared reporting platforms, and cheaper access to accredited verifiers, making compliance easier. Since many of the affected parties are developing countries, these funds could also support joint programmes on emissions reporting, technology upgrades, and supply chain transparency. This would lower adjustment costs and help keep CBAM credible as a climate policy and not a trade barrier.

India’s CCTS, notified in June 2023 under the amended Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act of 2022, is the most direct step towards reducing CBAM liability.[55] The Indian Carbon Market Portal was launched in March 2026, with CCTS in force for about 490 entities across seven energy-intensive sectors and formal trading of Carbon Credit Certificates to roll out in October 2026.[56],[57] Under Article 9 of CBAM, carbon prices already paid in the exporting country can be deducted from the levy.[58] This is possible only if the mechanism is mandatory, sector-wise, and produces a verifiable price per tonne. In its current form, CCTS is unlikely to qualify under EU requirements as it is intensity-based. This means that firms earn credits for doing better than a set baseline rather than putting a clear, fixed price on every tonne of carbon they emit. Introducing a price floor is one solution, and India’s CCTS already includes an indicative price collar. However, as CCTS is still in the early stages, the floor and ceiling prices have not yet been formally determined.[59] Until the price signal is transparent and verifiable enough to meet EU standards, Indian exporters cannot claim an offset against their CBAM liability.

Domestic reform alone is not enough. Even a well-designed CCTS will not automatically qualify for CBAM recognition, as the EU has yet to publish clear, binding criteria for when another country’s carbon pricing counts as equivalent. India will have to negotiate this directly with the EU. A clear mutual recognition framework should define the conditions under which CCTS credits are recognised against CBAM liabilities.

India should engage the EU to seek temporary transition flexibilities, such as fair phase-in timelines, partial exemptions, cooperation on data and digital systems, or recognition of domestic carbon payments. Similar to what has been discussed with the United States (US), India could demand comparable treatment.[60],[61] This would give Indian firms more time to adjust without weakening the CBAM’s climate goals.

As more countries tighten scrap exports to support their circular economies, access to scrap is becoming a major constraint for downstream producers. India should explore bilateral or regional agreements with scrap-rich countries, particularly Turkey, Japan, Russia, or the US, to secure stable and transparent metal scrap supply.[62] Such arrangements could support lower-emission secondary steel production and reduce input volatility for small manufacturers, since the segment is largely MSME-dominant.

Launched by Brazil at COP30, the IFCCT is a new multilateral space where climate and trade policy can be discussed together, outside the rigid silos of the UNFCCC and WTO.[63] India should use this platform actively, not just to voice its opposition to CBAM, but to make concrete proposals on CBDR-consistent carbon price recognition standards, transition support for MSME exporters in developing countries, and call for a pause on downstream CBAM expansion until developing countries have the tools and capacity to comply. A platform like this is both necessary and timely, at a moment when the boundaries between climate and trade policies have increasingly blurred.
When taken together, these measures could allow MSMEs to adjust gradually rather than face abrupt exclusion, and help them move towards cleaner and more transparent manufacturing.

The proposal to extend CBAM to downstream steel and aluminium products changes how the EU applies carbon pricing across value chains. While the policy aims to reduce value chain carbon leakage, it places the heaviest burden on MSMEs. Many smaller firms struggle to comply with the guidelines. This is not due to a lack of willingness to decarbonise but limited financial and technical capacity.

Early signs already point to trade disruptions, especially for exporters in developing economies. India—the world’s second-largest crude steel producer, with two-thirds of steel exports going to Europe—is particularly affected. This is because much of India’s steel production remains carbon-intensive. MSMEs also lack the capacity for timely emissions reporting. Without simpler reporting standards and targeted subsidies, downstream CBAM risks excluding MSMEs from EU-linked markets. With the right adjustments, however, it could still support a more gradual and inclusive low-carbon transition.

[8] In a supply chain, Tier-1 suppliers directly supply final components and products to final manufacturers or buyers. Tier-2 suppliers are suppliers or subcontractors to Tier-1, and Tier-3 suppliers serve Tier-2 in the same way. MSMEs in India's steel and aluminium sector are typically placed at Tier-2 and Tier-3, and are involved in metal processing, fabrication and re-rolling. They are furthest from the EU buyer but still pulled into compliance through the chain above them.
